## Question
What was the maiden surname of Ellen (born about 1868), who married Michael Doyle on 12 June 1889 in Dubuque, Dubuque County, Iowa?

## Conclusion (not proved)
The maiden surname is not established by the evidence gathered so far. The only record in hand is the marriage certificate, and its bride's surname is illegible. The finding is **not proved**. No candidate surname is offered, because none has any evidentiary basis.

## Evidence
**Marriage certificate.** Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate, Michael Doyle and Ellen [surname illegible], 12 June 1889; Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch. (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDOYLE-1889, accessed 2026-06-01.) The source is an original record.

- The groom's name, Michael Doyle, is legible. The bride's given name, Ellen, is legible. The date and place of the marriage are legible and consistent. Together these are direct evidence of the marriage. The information is primary and stated, with the bride and groom as informants to the recorder.
- The bride's surname is illegible in the register image because of the clerk's hand and fading. Her parents' names are also illegible. The surname is therefore not recoverable from this record as examined.
- Identity: the bride is linked to the tree person Ellen Doyle (I1), and the groom to Michael Doyle (I2). Her married name Doyle follows from the marriage itself.

## Conflicts
No conflicting sources exist. There is simply no usable evidence on the target attribute.

## Why not higher
The question's target, the maiden surname, rests on a single record in which it cannot be read, with no independent corroboration. That is not enough to favor any answer, so the tier is not proved. Not-proved is a statement about the current evidence. It does not say the surname cannot be found.

## What could resolve it
The maiden surname remains unresolved pending records that were not searched. These are: the 1900 and 1910 censuses and Iowa state censuses for the couple; birth or baptism records of their children, which commonly name the mother's maiden surname; death records and obituaries for Ellen or Michael Doyle; Dubuque Catholic parish registers; a Dubuque County marriage index or clerk's register; and another copy or better image of the certificate. A legible index reading of the same certificate would be the quickest check.

## Tree
Nothing was encoded about the maiden surname, because there is no concluded value. The tree keeps Ellen's married name, Doyle.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
When and where did Anders Monsen (b. 1759, christened Hamre 7 April 1759; d. 1821 Åsebø) marry Unna Halsteinsdatter (christened Hamre 27 May 1745), and what does the marriage record show?

## Conclusion
The evidence indicates, at a probable level, that Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter married on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway.

## Evidence
The one record found is the index entry "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register. It names the groom as Anders Monsen and the bride as "Urna Halsteinsdr", and gives the date 25 Jun 1786 and place Hamre.

**Classification.** The source is a derivative index of an original parish register entry. The information is primary: the event was recorded by the parish clerk or minister in the course of official duty at the time of the marriage (informant proximity: official duty), and the names are stated, with the couple as the underlying subjects. The evidence is direct for the date, place and identity of the spouses. The index is index-only: no image reference was returned and no record read was made, so no digitized image is claimed.

**Identity.** The groom's name matches Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH), and the place, Hamre, is the parish where he was christened in 1759. The bride's indexed name "Urna Halsteinsdr" is a transcription variant (u/n confusion, abbreviated patronymic) of Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX), who was christened at Hamre on 27 May 1745 according to the starting tree. No competing candidates or conflicts were registered.

**Starting tree.** The starting tree already carries a Couple relationship (rel-anders-unna) between the two. It had no marriage fact and no linked source; this record supplies both the date and place.

## Caveats
Unna was about 14 years older than Anders (she was about 41 and he about 27 in 1786). This is unusual but not impossible, and nothing in the record contradicts it. The conclusion rests on one derivative index entry; it has not been compared with the original Hamre register or a second index. Checking the 1786 Hamre marriage register image or Digitalarkivet transcription, and examining the remaining 48 search hits, would corroborate it and could raise the tier.

## Tier
Probable: direct, primary information from a single derivative source, with no conflicts, but research is not exhaustive.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908)? An unsourced online family tree names him, and several other trees repeat the claim without citing a record.

## Conclusion
Disproved. Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was not Patrick Flynn's father. He was buried on 14 November 1842, about three years before Patrick's birth. This finding concerns this candidate only. It does not say who Patrick's father was.

## Evidence
**The candidate's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842. The entry is an original record. It was made by the officiating priest as part of his duty, and the information is primary (a_003, a_004). The register gives the townland, an age of about 42 and a wife, Bridget. These match the man the online tree names, so the entry identifies the right Thomas. Citation: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**The subject's birth.** The 1850 U.S. census shows Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of widow Bridget Flynn in Schuylkill County, with no adult male Flynn present. This points to a birth about 1845 (a_001, a_002). The informant is unknown, so the age is indirect information of undetermined quality. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The 1908 death certificate independently gives an age of about 63 at death on 12 March 1908. That also points to a birth about 1845. Its informant was Patrick's son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at the birth, so the age is secondary information (a_005, a_006). Citation: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026.

## Correlation
The two age statements come from different records, enumerators and informants. They agree on a birth around 1844-1845. Even allowing generously for age errors, neither supports a birth before about 1843. A child born after the father's death can arrive no later than roughly nine months after it, which here means about August 1843. A birth in 1843 or later therefore cannot be reconciled with a father buried in November 1842 unless both age statements are wrong by two years or more in the same direction. Neither record names Patrick's father. The father is the point in dispute, so the evidence here is indirect, but it is a chronological impossibility, not a matter of weighing.

## Conflicts and limits
No conflicting evidence was found, and no conflict is registered. The widowed Bridget Flynn in the 1850 household shares a first name with the wife in the burial entry. That is a lead for a new question about Patrick's actual parentage. It does not support the claimed father, because the burial date rules him out on the evidence gathered. A baptism entry for Patrick, not yet searched, would fix his birth year directly and could only confirm or very slightly narrow this timeline. As with any conclusion, a record not yet found could change it, but no known evidence points that way.

## Tier
Disproved. An original primary record places the candidate's death before the subject's birth, and two independent age statements place the birth after it. The tree therefore carries no Thomas-to-Patrick relationship.

The two age statements come from different records, enumerators and informants. They agree on a birth around 1844-1845. Even allowing generously for age errors, neither supports a birth before about 1843. A child born after the father's death can arrive no later than roughly nine months after it, which here means about August 1843. A birth in 1843 or later therefore cannot be reconciled with a father buried in November 1842 unless both age statements are wrong by two years or more in the same direction. Neither record names Patrick's father. The father is the point in dispute, so the evidence here is indirect, but it is a chronological impossibility, not a matter of weighing.

## Conflicts and limits
No conflicting evidence was found, and no conflict is registered. The widowed Bridget Flynn in the 1850 household shares a first name with the wife in the burial entry. That is a lead for a new question about Patrick's actual parentage. It does not support the claimed father, because the burial date rules him out on the evidence gathered. A baptism entry for Patrick, not yet searched, would fix his birth year directly and could only confirm or very slightly narrow this timeline. As with any conclusion, a record not yet found could change it, but no known evidence points that way.

## Tier
Disproved. An original primary record places the candidate's death before the subject's birth, and two independent age statements place the birth after it. The tree therefore carries no Thomas-to-Patrick relationship.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
When and where did Anders Monsen (b. 1759, christened Hamre) marry Unna Halsteinsdatter (christened 27 May 1745, Hamre), and what does the marriage record show?

## Conclusion
The evidence indicates that Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter married on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway. This is a probable conclusion, not a proved one, because it rests on one derivative index entry and the register image has not been examined.

## Evidence
The FamilySearch index entry names the groom as Anders Monsen and the bride as 'Urna Halsteinsdr', and gives the marriage as 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway, citing the Hamre prestegjeld parish register. Source citation: "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register.

**Classification.** The source is a derivative index of an original church book. The date and place are primary information, stated directly (direct evidence) by the officiating minister or parish clerk acting in official duty at the time of the event. The names are stated by the parties themselves, who were present as groom and bride.

**Identity.** The groom's name, sex and parish match Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH), christened 7 April 1759 at Hamre kirke. The bride's indexed surname 'Halsteinsdr' is a standard abbreviation or transcription of Halsteinsdatter. It matches Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX), christened 27 May 1745 at Hamre, and the existing couple relationship in the tree. Both are linked by person-evidence.

## Conflicts and limits
No conflicting evidence was found, and no conflict is registered. The weaknesses are these: one source only; a derivative index rather than the register itself; and a spelling variant of the bride's given name (Urna for Unna), most plausibly a transcription or reading difference in the handwriting. **Digital image:** the project has not confirmed that a digitized image of the register page exists or is accessible. The search result carried no image reference and the record was never opened with record_read, so this narrative does not state that an image is available. The link above is the index record, not a confirmed image. Whether the register page can be viewed is the first thing to check.

## What would raise the tier
Opening the record (record_read) to check for a linked image, and reading the Hamre register page itself, would confirm the transcription and show any witnesses or residences. Banns or a second parish copy of the register, if indexed, would add an independent check.

## Tier
Probable. Direct, primary-information evidence with no contradiction, but a single derivative source and an unexamined original.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Who were the parents of John Richardson, who is recorded in the project tree as born 24 July 1833 (Preston, Lancashire) and baptised 25 September 1833 at Ashton-under-Lyne?

## Conclusion (probable)
The evidence strongly suggests that John Richardson was the son of Thomas Richardson, a spinner, and Mary Mallalieu, who married on 12 November 1826. The tier is probable, not proved, because the register year (1832) differs from the tree year (1833), so the identity of the baptised child with the tree subject rests on a stated assumption of a one-year discrepancy.

## Evidence
**Baptism register (original, primary information).** Entry no. 2040 in the St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, dated 25 September 1832, records John, son of Thomas X (his mark) Richardson, Spinner, and Mary, Town (Ashton-under-Lyne), recorded by the officiating curate J. Hardman as part of his duty. Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254-255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674. This is an original source with primary information and direct evidence naming both parents. The entry records the mother only as Mary. The name Mallalieu is not in the baptism entry; it comes from the marriage record below.

**Index of the same baptism (derivative).** "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm. It names Thomas Richardson and Mary and carries the same 1832 date, so the 1832 reading is the register's date and not an indexing slip.

**Marriage register (original, primary information).** Walton le Dale, St Leonard, marriage register p. 228, entry no. 684: Thos Richardson, Bachelor, and Mary Mallalieu, Spinster, married by banns on 12 November 1826 by Rev. Henry Fielden, Sub Curate; both signed by mark. Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm. Its indexed copy (src_002, derivative) agrees. This supplies the maiden name. ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

## Conclusion
The evidence indicates that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. This is a **probable** conclusion. Patrick's mother is not identified by any record found so far; that claim is **not proved**.

## Evidence for paternity
1. **1908 death certificate.** Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It states "Father: Thomas Flynn." The record is an original; the informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth, so the parentage information is secondary, though stated directly.
2. **1850 census.** 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. Patrick appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, head. The 1850 census does not state relationships, so a child relationship is inferred from household position and shared surname (indirect evidence; informant unknown). The Ancestry index of the same census (dwelling 84, Thomas Flynn household) is a derivative copy and adds no independent weight.
3. **1860 census.** 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 15, is again in Thomas Flynn's household in the same county. The relationship is again inferred (indirect), and the informant is probably the same household member as in 1850.

The three records are separate originals created by different enumerators and a different civil office, and they agree. The direct statement of the death certificate and the repeated co-residence reinforce each other. The weaknesses are that the direct statement is secondary information and the census evidence is only inferential.

## Conflict
Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved. The son-in-law's report of Pennsylvania is judged an error by a distant informant. It does not bear on identity here, since the name, county and father's name agree across records, and it is accounted for rather than left open.

## Maternity
No assertion names Patrick's mother. No wife of Thomas Flynn is identified in the evidence gathered. Maternity remains unanswered pending a baptism or parish record for Patrick, a marriage record for Thomas Flynn, or the 1880 census.

## Limits
The tier is probable, not proved, because the direct evidence is secondary and the rest is inferred, and because Thomas Flynn's probate file, parish records and later censuses have not been searched. They would mostly corroborate paternity and could identify the mother. Tree fact F3 (Thomas Flynn, birth about 1818, Ireland) carries no linked source entry in the project.

- **Gate:** Every assertion on q_001 has a reasoned classification. Patrick (I1) and Thomas (I2) each carry a linked identity assertion. The only conflict, c_001 (birthplace), is resolved and doesn't bear on identity, so it doesn't block.
- **Summary:** `ps_001` is a new summary with a paternity claim at `probable`. It rests on the 1908 death certificate, which names Thomas Flynn as father but comes from a secondary informant, and on the 1850 and 1860 census co-residence, which is only inferred. Maternity is not proved because no record names a mother. That part is covered in the narrative, not as its own claim.
- **Question:** q_001 is marked resolved. I did not set the project to `completed`, because q_002 and h_001 still have no proof summary.

- **Limits:** Not yet searched are Thomas's probate file, a baptism or parish record, a Thomas Flynn marriage record, and the 1870 and 1880 censuses. The probate file and later censuses would mostly corroborate paternity. The parish and marriage records are the likeliest way to name the mother.
- **Next step:** Run proof-conclusion on q_002 (and h_001). Plan the searches that would raise the tier (probate, parish, marriage, 1880 census) in research-plan.

---

Patrick Flynn's father was most likely Thomas Flynn, an Irish-born man living in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. This finding is likely, not certain. Patrick's 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father, but the informant was his son-in-law, who wasn't there at Patrick's birth. Patrick also appears in Thomas's household in the 1850 and 1860 censuses, which fits a father and son but doesn't state the relationship. The records disagree on where Patrick was born (Ireland in the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate). I judged the censuses more reliable, and the disagreement doesn't affect who his father was. Patrick's mother has not been identified. Not yet searched are Thomas's estate papers, church baptism and marriage records, and the 1870 and 1880 censuses.

Next, the other open question about Patrick's whereabouts in the 1850 census needs its own conclusion, and the searches that could confirm his father and find his mother can be planned.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)? An unsourced online family tree, repeated by several other trees, says so.

## Conclusion
**Disproved.** Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was buried on 14 November 1842, about three years before Patrick was born. He cannot have been Patrick's father. This finding is limited to that one man. It does not say who Patrick's parents were.

## Evidence
**Thomas's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842. It is an original register entry made by the officiating priest, whose duty was to record the burial (primary information, stated directly). The entry gives the townland and wife's name (Bridget) that match the Thomas Flynn the online tree names, so this is the man the claim refers to. Citation: "Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026."

**Patrick's birth.** The 1850 census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present. Citation: "1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026." The informant is unknown, so the age is of indeterminate quality, and it is an inferred birth year (about 1845). Patrick's 1908 death certificate independently gives an age of about 63, supplied by his son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at the birth (secondary information, calculated). Citation: "Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026." The certificate does not name his father.

## Reasoning
Both age statements are imprecise and could each be off by a year or two. Even so, they agree with each other, and a birth in 1843 or later is the earliest either allows. A child born after Thomas's November 1842 burial could not be his, even allowing for a posthumous birth, because that would put Patrick's birth no later than about August 1843. That would make him 7 in the 1850 census and about 65 at death, which neither record supports. The evidence is consistent and no conflict was recorded. The reasoning rests on a death date in an original register, which is far stronger than the tree claim, which cites no record.

## What this does not settle
The widow Bridget in Patrick's 1850 household shares a wife's name with the burial entry. That is noted but not used: a shared first name is not enough to say Bridget was Thomas's widow, and it does not make Thomas Patrick's father. Patrick's parentage remains unidentified. A baptismal record for Patrick or Schuylkill County records for Bridget Flynn could address it. Research may be reopened if new evidence appears, but a death three years before the birth is not overturned by anything now conceivable for this candidate.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

agent_returns.text:
Assessment only. I wrote nothing to the project.

**Bottom line:** ps_001 is rated probable with a shortfall of "gap". That tier is defensible for the father, Thomas Flynn. The proof is not proved, and it doesn't claim to be. It has some mechanical and wording flaws, listed below.

**1. Reasonably exhaustive research (incomplete, as the proof says).**
- Searched: the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage), the 1860 census and the 1908 death certificate.
- Not searched, as the proof itself says: the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses.
- The 1880 census is the first to state relationships. It would be the first direct census statement of parentage.
- Nothing addresses the mother. The question asks for "parents", but ps_001 concludes only the father. It should say so or split the claim into father and mother.

**2. Citations (met).**
- The three citations match the stored citations for src_001, src_003 and src_004 verbatim.
- The narrative does not cite the Ancestry record (src_002), which is derivative. That is fine.

**3. Analysis and correlation (mostly met, with weaknesses).**
- The classifications of a_004, a_010 and a_013 are reasoned, and the narrative is honest that the census evidence is indirect. The 1850 and 1860 relationship assertions are inferred, with indeterminate information. The death certificate's father entry is stated, but the information is secondary (informant: son-in-law James Brown).
- "Three independent lines of evidence" is overstated. The two censuses are indirect and probably share one informant, a household member. The certificate is the only direct statement, and its informant is secondary.
- The proof calls the certificate "direct evidence" and also "secondary". Both are true, but it should be weighted as a single secondary statement.
- The proof's statement that the 1860 census "relationship column was not introduced until 1880" is correct.

**4. Conflict resolution (substantively met, with one record defect).**
- c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved, with reasoning. The ps_001 narrative accounts for it.
- Birthplace is an identifying attribute, because it bears on whether the census Patrick and the 1908 decedent are the same man. Yet c_001 has an empty `blocks_question_ids`, so it is not formally tied to q_001. That should be corrected.
- The proof does not say what tied the 1908 decedent to the census boy besides the name. The certificate gives only Thomas as father. It does not name a mother, a Schuylkill County residence history or an age that matches. If the 1881 deed, the will or the obituary links the two men, the identity argument becomes firmer.
- The resolution rests on "two contemporary sources", but the proof elsewhere concedes they share one informant. That weakens the weighing a little.

**5. Soundly reasoned, coherent conclusion (mostly met).**
- The proof is organized and its limits are stated.
- "Probably the son" is consistent with probable.
- The `exhaustive_search_summary` says "probate search in progress", but no probate log entry exists. I read that as a search that was planned, not performed.
- The proof carries no `claims[]` breakdown. The project already flags this.

**Tree.** R1 (Thomas Flynn → Patrick Flynn) is encoded, with sources S1, S2 and S3. The Birth fact (about 1845, Ireland) is marked primary, which agrees with the conflict resolution.

**Evidence gaps for the next round (not defects of ps_001).**
These records exist in research.json but have no extracted assertions and no log entries. They are not cited in ps_001.
- **src_005, the 1845 St. Mary's, Pottsville baptism.** It could name both parents. It also bears on the birthplace dispute, since a Pottsville baptism in 1845 would support Pennsylvania over Ireland. It could raise the tier, or complicate c_001.
- **src_006, the 1881 will of Thomas Flynn.** If it names Patrick as a son, that is direct testimony from the father himself. That would be the main route to proved.
- **src_008, the 1881 deed from Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn.** It supports a relationship, but only if the deed states one.
- **src_009, the 1908 obituary in the Pottsville Republican.** It might name the parents or the birthplace.
- **src_007, the 1905 birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn.** It is probably a descendant's record and is weak for this question.
- These sources also carry rough working citations that need repair before use.
- The tree already cites S5 (the baptism register) on R2 and R3, the sibling links, so the baptism has been seen in some form.

Any of the will, baptism or deed, once extracted and found to name Patrick as Thomas's son, would likely lift the father claim to proved, provided c_001 stays resolved. The 1870 and 1880 censuses would corroborate rather than narrow the answer.

**Next step:** re-run proof-conclusion on q_001 after record-extraction covers src_005, src_006, src_008 and src_009.

---

The existing proof concludes that Thomas Flynn was very likely Patrick Flynn's father. Patrick was born around 1845 and died in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania in 1908. The finding rests on two census records that list Patrick in Thomas's household, and a 1908 death certificate that names Thomas as his father. The certificate's information came from Patrick's son-in-law, who was not a witness to the birth. The proof is solid for a likely answer but not for a firm one. The census records never state the relationship, and the proof says nothing about Patrick's mother. It did not examine the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses, or several other records that are already in the project. Those records are an 1845 baptism, Thomas's 1881 will, an 1881 deed from Thomas to Patrick, and Patrick's 1908 obituary.

Next, those unexamined records should be read and the proof re-run, which could make the finding well established.

The existing finding is that Patrick Flynn was probably the son of Thomas Flynn. It rests on three records. The 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick in Thomas's household, but neither census states the relationship. The 1908 death certificate names Thomas as father, but the informant was Patrick's son-in-law, who was reporting second-hand. The next step is to analyze those found records, then rewrite the proof with named records and citations, and add the later censuses and probate to the search plan.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn.

### Evidence Summary

The conclusion rests on a_004, a_010, and a_013, drawn from src_001, src_003, and
src_004. Taken together these assertions are consistent with a parent-child
relationship and none of them contradicts it.

### Conflict Resolution

c_001 was resolved in favour of the earlier of the two record groups, on the usual
preponderance grounds. See the conflict entry for the full reasoning.

### Assessment

Rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because the supporting assertions listed
above are not all direct, and because plan_001 has open items outstanding. Advancing
the tier would require the records named in the plan.

agent_returns.text:
**Assessment of ps_001 (q_001, parentage of Patrick Flynn): probable tier is defensible, but the write-up does not meet the standard as written.** Nothing was written to the project. This is a review only.

**Preconditions.** Every assertion tied to q_001 has a reasoned classification. Patrick (I1) and Thomas (I2) are each identified by linked records. c_001 is a birthplace conflict, resolved, and it blocks no question. Nothing stops a conclusion here.

**1. Tier: probable is right for the father, and it is the ceiling for this evidence.**
- The evidence has three supports:
  - The 1850 census (a_004) lists Patrick in Thomas's household. That is an inferred relationship, because the 1850 census does not state relationships.
  - The 1860 census (a_010) is the same kind of evidence.
  - The 1908 death certificate (a_013) names Thomas as father. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, so this is secondary information.
- No direct, primary statement of parentage is cited, so proved is not available.
- Possible would be too low. The three items agree, nothing contradicts them, and the identity is consistent.
- The question asks for the parents, plural, and the proof covers only the father. No mother is named or analyzed. The proof should say so, or carry a per-parent breakdown. The project's own status note already flags that ps_001 states no claims.

**2. Self-containment: fails.**
- The narrative names its evidence only by bare ids (a_004, a_010, a_013, src_001, src_003, src_004, c_001, plan_001).
- A reader without the project file cannot tell what the records are. The narrative should name the 1850 and 1860 censuses (with dwelling and family numbers) and the 1908 death certificate no. 4521, and name James Brown as informant.
- It never states the three-layer classification (source, information, evidence). It never says that the census relationships are inferred from household position, or that the death certificate informant was secondary.
- Its reason for stopping at probable ("not all direct", "plan_001 has open items") is vague. It should say that no direct primary statement exists and name the records that could supply one.

**3. Citations: fails.** The narrative has no inline citations. The stored citations for src_001, src_003 and src_004 are complete and should be copied in verbatim.

**4. Conflicts: partly met.**
- c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved on sound grounds. The informant was secondary, and the death certificate came 63 years after the birth.
- The narrative only says it was "resolved in favour of the earlier … record group, on the usual preponderance grounds." It does not state the attribute, the competing values, or the reasoning, and it does not say that the dispute is not about identity.
- The conflict prefers a_002 as the birthplace, which is not among the proof's supporting ids. The 1850 and 1860 informants are probably the same person, which weakens the "two sources" weighing. The proof should say this.
- The hypothesis note calls the three items "three independent pieces of evidence", which overstates it. The two censuses are the same household and probably the same informant, and both are inferred. The proof should not repeat that wording.

**5. Exhaustiveness: partly met, and the stated scope is stale.**
- The scope names the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage), the 1860 census, and the death certificate. The MyHeritage search returned nothing, and the summary should say so.
- The Ancestry record (src_002) is derivative, and the proof does not use it. The summary should not list it as independent corroboration.
- "Probate search in progress" and "1870, 1880, 1900 not yet searched" are unfinished. The 1880 census is the one that matters most: it is the first census with a stated relationship column, so it could give direct evidence of Patrick's father.
- The shortfall of `gap` is correct, because reachable records remain unsearched.
- Those unsearched records would corroborate an answer that already exists. They would not narrow it, so they do not cap the tier at possible. A direct 1880 relationship or a parentage statement in a probate record could raise the tier to proved.

**6. Unresolvability claims.** None are made. The narrative says that advancing the tier "would require the records named in the plan", and it should name them.

**7. Tree: father encoded, mother absent.**
- I2 (Thomas) is Patrick's parent, and Mary (I3) and James (I4) are also listed as Thomas's children.
- The ParentChild link to Thomas matches the probable tier.
- No mother exists in the tree.

**Gaps outside the current proof.** These are not defects in ps_001.
- src_005 to src_009 are logged and have zero assertions extracted. They are:
  - the 1845 baptism at St. Mary's, Pottsville
  - the 1881 will of Thomas Flynn
  - the 1881 deed from Thomas to Patrick
  - the 1908 obituary
  - the 1905 birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn
- The will, the deed and the baptism could directly state or imply the father-son relationship. If extracted and correlated, they could support proved. They are the biggest opportunity to raise the tier.
- The baptism might also name the mother.
- The baptism and the Pennsylvania birthplace could re-open the Ireland versus Pennsylvania question, depending on what the register says.
- Those five sources also carry rough citations that need completing.
- Assertions a_005, a_006 and a_007 are not used in the proof, and the 1850 name assertions add nothing to the question.
- q_002 (Patrick's 1850 census location) is resolved but has no proof summary.

**Recommended next step.** Run record-extraction on src_005 to src_009, then re-run proof-conclusion on q_001. The re-run should rewrite the narrative with named records, inline citations and an explicit account of c_001, and it should state the mother as unresolved. Searches for the 1870 and 1880 censuses and for probate should go through research-plan.

---

The existing finding is that Patrick Flynn was probably the son of Thomas Flynn. It rests on three records. The 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick in Thomas's household, but neither census states the relationship. The 1908 death certificate names Thomas as father, but the informant was Patrick's son-in-law, who was reporting second-hand. The finding is sound and the evidence is consistent, but it is still only "likely". The written proof is hard to follow without the project files, because it names records by internal codes, cites none of them, and does not explain why the birthplace disagreement was resolved the way it was. It also says nothing about Patrick's mother. Not yet searched: the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and probate records. A baptism, a will, a deed and an obituary have been found but not yet analyzed.

The next step is to analyze those found records, then rewrite the proof with named records and citations, and add the later censuses and probate to the search plan.

## Question
When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born about 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Status: attempt recorded, conclusion blocked at the identity-linking stage

Content note: none; this is an ordinary probate matter.

**What the evidence shows.** The 1885 term order book of the Muhlenberg County Court records the administration of the intestate estate of an Elijah Wilkins, deceased, with Jesse Wilkins as administrator (Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, Court Order Books, administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, Jesse Wilkins administrator, 1885 term; digital images, FamilySearch.org). This is a derivative index of the order-book page. Its information quality is indeterminate: the informant was the county clerk and his proximity to the death is unknown. It states no death date, so at most it brackets a death before the 1885 term, in Muhlenberg County. A search of Kentucky statewide death collections found nothing, as expected, since statewide registration began in 1911 and no certificate exists for a man last documented in 1870.

**Why no conclusion is drawn.** The decedent is tied to our subject only through the administrator, Jesse Wilkins, who is the subject's son in the tree (I2). No identity link yet shows that the administrator named in the record is that Jesse. The one link of the estate itself to the subject (the decedent's name) is held at speculative confidence because a second Elijah Wilkins, born about 1822, lived in Muhlenberg County. Until the administrator is tied to I2 and the second Elijah is excluded, the estate cannot validly be correlated with the subject.

**Tier: not proved.** Identity of the decedent with the subject is not established by the evidence gathered so far. The bracket (died before 1885 in Muhlenberg County, after 1870) remains a candidate only. It could be settled by linking the administrator Jesse Wilkins to I2 (person-evidence), and by Muhlenberg County probate packets, settlement or inventory records, or burial records that name the decedent's residence, age or heirs.

entry.narrative_markdown:
# Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ca. 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Conclusion.** The evidence points to Thomas Flynn (b. ca. 1818, Ireland) as Patrick's father; this is *probable*, not proved. Patrick's mother is *not proved*: the only candidate, Bridget Flynn, is tied to the family by nothing but a common surname.

## Paternity: Thomas Flynn (probable)

1. **1850 census.** Patrick Flynn appears in the household of Thomas Flynn (head), Schuylkill County, dwelling 84, family 91 (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026). The source is an original. The 1850 census does not state relationships, so the child relationship is inferred from household position and surname: the information is indeterminate, the informant unknown, and the basis inferred (indirect evidence). The Ancestry index of the same census is a derivative of that one original and adds no independent weight.
2. **1860 census.** Patrick, age 15, is again in a Thomas Flynn household (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). Same classification: original source, relationship inferred, informant unknown. It shows continuity of the co-residence ten years on, which makes a boarder or unrelated lodger less likely but does not state kinship. The two censuses likely share the household informant.
3. **1908 death certificate.** Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It names the father as Thomas Flynn. This is the only direct statement of parentage, but the informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, who was not present at the birth and reported secondhand (secondary information). It is original and stated, but it comes 63 years after the 1850 census and from a generation removed.

These three items agree and nothing contradicts them, but they are not three independent direct statements: two are inferences from one household, and the one direct statement is secondary. That is a strong preponderance for a probable finding, short of proved.

## Conflict accounted for

Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favour of Ireland: two contemporary census entries outweigh a son-in-law's later recollection. It does not call into question that the census Patrick and the decedent are the same man, since name, county and age all agree, and the death certificate's father's name matches the census head.

## Maternity: not proved

The 1870 census lists Bridget Flynn as a widow aged 52 heading a household in Schuylkill County (1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026). The census names no husband, lists no children, and does not mention Patrick or Thomas. The link between her and Thomas Flynn rests only on a shared surname, which is common in this county; the identity link was scored 0.0002 and rated speculative. Her age, 52 in 1870 (born ca. 1818), is also the same as Thomas's, which does not exclude a marriage but does not support one. The baptism entries at St. Patrick's, Pottsville (10 April 1870 and 22 September 1872) name Patrick Flynn and Mary Doyle as parents of Patrick's own children, so they concern his wife, not his mother, and give no evidence about his mother. Given names of Patrick's children are not treated as evidence of his parentage. No record names Patrick's mother. Her identity remains unresolved pending Thomas Flynn's probate or death record, Patrick's marriage record, or an obituary, any of which could name her. No relationship to Bridget is encoded.

## What would raise the tier

The following reachable records would corroborate paternity: Schuylkill County probate or estate records for Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as heir, the 1880 census (which states relationships), Patrick's marriage record, and an obituary. Thomas Flynn's death or burial record is the record most likely to narrow the maternal answer.

**Tier: probable (paternity); not proved (maternity). Overall: probable.** Findings may be revised if new evidence appears.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Did Person A (born 1856, Germany) leave an accessible South Dakota death certificate, and when did Person A die?

## Answer
A death certificate is **not accessible** in the records searched so far, and Person A **probably died in 1935 at or near Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota**, with the possibility of early 1936 not excluded by the age evidence. The exact day is not established. This is a *possible* answer (tier: possible), because both supporting sources give secondary or undetermined information and the one record type that would settle the date has not been reached.

## Evidence
**Find a Grave Index** (derivative; "Find a Grave Index," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVLD-NSQ7 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, memorial #88075502). An unidentified contributor states birth 1856, death 1935, burial Gregory, South Dakota. Informant and basis are unknown, so the information quality is indeterminate.

**South Dakota Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942** (original record, but the informant, a WPA grave-registration worker, is unidentified: "South Dakota, Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942," database with images, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:CYCQ-NRW2 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota). It records burial at Gregory (IOOF Cemetery), male, non-veteran, age at death 79, and a blank death date. The age is indirect evidence: with a birth year of 1856 (tree fact F1, Birth, Germany, 1856, a starting-tree fact that carries no linked source entry in the project), age 79 puts the death in 1935 or, if the birthday fell late in the year, up to the following year. It agrees with the Find a Grave year and does not contradict it. The two sources are not fully independent of each other as to the year, since the grave-registration age depends on the same unknown informant knowledge; the Grave Registration compilation (1939-1942) also establishes only that the death preceded about 1942.

Tree fact F2 (Residence, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota, 1935) places the subject in Gregory in 1935, consistent with both sources; it also carries no linked source entry in the project.

## The certificate
Two searches of FamilySearch-indexed South Dakota death records under two spelling variants returned nothing for Person A (log_003, log_004). This shows no certificate is *indexed and findable on FamilySearch*; it does not show that none exists. South Dakota has had statewide death registration since the early twentieth century, so a 1935 certificate was probably created. Unindexed film for browsing and the South Dakota State Archives / state vital records office have not been consulted, so whether a certificate is accessible by those routes remains unresolved pending those searches.

## Conflicts
None registered; the sources agree on year and place.

## Conclusion and limits
Person A died probably in 1935 (secondary and indirect evidence; possibly into early 1936 on the age alone), buried at Gregory, South Dakota. Whether an accessible death certificate exists is not established by the evidence gathered so far; browsing unindexed Gregory County death records for 1935-1936 or requesting the certificate from the State Archives could establish both the exact date and the certificate's existence. A certificate could also refine or contradict the year. Family tree file contents on FamilySearch were not changed.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845 in Ireland, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion: not proved.** The evidence gathered so far does not favor either of two candidate fathers, Thomas Flynn or Michael Flynn. No father is concluded and nothing is written to the tree.

### The subject is firmly identified at death, but not in childhood
The death certificate (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026) is an original record with primary information on the death: the attending physician stated the date, 12 March 1908. It leaves the father blank. The informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the father as unknown. That is negative evidence from a secondhand informant, and it does not point to either candidate.

The 1860 census (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026) shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, a boarder and coal laborer. No Flynn adult lived in the household, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears nearby. It places the adult Patrick in the right county, but it does not connect him to either 1850 household.

### Two equally plausible childhood households
Two original 1850 census records each show a Patrick Flynn of fitting age and Irish birth in Schuylkill County.

- Candidate A: age 5, in the household of Thomas Flynn (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). This implies birth about 1845.
- Candidate B: age 6, in the household of Michael Flynn (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). This implies birth about 1844, within normal census age error.

The 1850 census does not state relationships. The child-to-head link in both is inferred from household position, and the informants are unknown. The information about each child is therefore of indeterminate quality, and the parentage is indirect. Each hypothesis (Thomas, Michael) rests on assuming that its child is the subject. Nothing in the record set tests that assumption, so neither is favored over the other. A given-name or age match does not separate them.

### Why no father is concluded
The death certificate and the 1860 census, the only records that tie the adult subject to a time and place, link to neither household. A search of Catholic parish registers (FamilySearch and the National Library of Ireland, Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850) returned no baptism naming a father. That repository coverage may simply not include the relevant register. There are no unresolved conflicts to account for. The problem is the absence of any bridge, not contradictory evidence.

The question is not established by the evidence gathered so far. It remains open pending record types not yet examined: Patrick's marriage record and his children's baptism, marriage or death records (which often name a grandfather), the 1870 and 1880 censuses, obituary and burial records for 1908, naturalization papers, and county probate files for Thomas or Michael Flynn. Any of these could name the father or place Patrick with one household.

### Tier
Not proved. Two candidates remain with indirect evidence only and no separating evidence.

## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845 in Ireland, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion: not proved.** The evidence gathered so far does not favor either of two candidate fathers, Thomas Flynn or Michael Flynn. No father is concluded and nothing is written to the tree.

### The subject is firmly identified at death, but not in childhood
The death certificate (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026) is an original record with primary information on the death: the attending physician stated the date, 12 March 1908. It leaves the father blank. The informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the father as unknown. That is negative evidence from a secondhand informant, and it does not point to either candidate.

The 1860 census (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026) shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, a boarder and coal laborer. No Flynn adult lived in the household, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears nearby. It places the adult Patrick in the right county, but it does not connect him to either 1850 household.

### Two equally plausible childhood households
Two original 1850 census records each show a Patrick Flynn of fitting age and Irish birth in Schuylkill County.

- Candidate A: age 5, in the household of Thomas Flynn (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). This implies birth about 1845.
- Candidate B: age 6, in the household of Michael Flynn (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). This implies birth about 1844, within normal census age error.

The 1850 census does not state relationships. The child-to-head link in both is inferred from household position, and the informants are unknown. The information about each child is therefore of indeterminate quality, and the parentage is indirect. Each hypothesis (Thomas, Michael) rests on assuming that its child is the subject. Nothing in the record set tests that assumption, so neither is favored over the other. An age match does not separate them.

### Why no father is concluded
The death certificate and the 1860 census, the only records that tie the adult subject to a time and place, link to neither household. A search of Catholic parish registers (FamilySearch and the National Library of Ireland, Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850) returned no baptism naming a father. That repository coverage may simply not include the relevant register. There are no unresolved conflicts to account for. The problem is the absence of any bridge, not contradictory evidence.

The question is not established by the evidence gathered so far. It remains open pending record types not yet examined: Patrick's marriage record and his children's baptism, marriage or death records (which often name a grandfather), the 1870 and 1880 censuses, obituary and burial records for 1908, naturalization papers, and county probate files for Thomas or Michael Flynn. Any of these could name the father or place Patrick with one household.

### Tier
Not proved. Two candidates remain with indirect evidence only and no separating evidence.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants would outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. That weighing has not been done: c_001 is unresolved, no preferred assertion is recorded, and this conclusion adopts no birthplace.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants would outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. That weighing has not been done: c_001 is unresolved, no preferred assertion is recorded, and this conclusion adopts no birthplace.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

ops.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845 in Ireland, died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

## Conclusion
Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland). The mother, named in the same two primary records as Mary (Maria) Brennan, is tracked as a separate question. Tier: proved.

## Evidence
**Direct, primary, original evidence (two independent sources).**
1. The baptismal register of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, County Tipperary, records on 12 March 1845 the baptism of Patricius Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan. The recorder was the officiating priest, Rev. Michael O'Connor, with the parents present, so the information on parentage is primary. Citation: St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church (County Tipperary, Ireland), baptismal register, entry for Patricius Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan, baptized 12 March 1845; National Library of Ireland Catholic Parish Registers, microfilm 04173/04, image 287; digital image, NationalLibrary.ie, accessed 4 May 2026.
2. The Flynn family Bible (Dublin imprint 1840) carries a birth entry for Patrick Flynn, b. 1845, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan, written by the father in a single consistent contemporaneous hand. It is original, primary and direct, and independent of the register (different recorder and record type). Its provenance ties it to our subject: it descended from Patrick Flynn (d. 1908, Schuylkill County) through his daughter, wife of James Brown, to a present descendant. Citation: Flynn family Bible (Holy Bible, Dublin imprint 1840), birth and family record pages, entry for Patrick Flynn, b. 1845, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan; original descended from Patrick Flynn (d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) through his daughter, the wife of James Brown, to its present holder, a descendant in her line; digital images examined 4 May 2026.

**Corroborating evidence.**
- 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, dwelling 84, family 91 (NARA M432, roll 810): Patrick Flynn is in the household of Thomas Flynn, head. Indirect: the 1850 census states no relationships, so the tie is inferred from household position and surname; the informant is unstated.
- 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, dwelling 112, family 119 (NARA M653, roll 1141): Patrick, age 15 (born about 1845, Ireland), is again in Thomas Flynn's household. Indirect for the same reason.
- Pennsylvania death certificate no. 4521 (1908): names Thomas Flynn as father. Direct, but secondary information, supplied by son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at the birth.
- The Ancestry 1850 index is a derivative copy of the same census and adds no independent weight.

## Identity
The Tipperary child (Patricius, 1845) and the Pennsylvania man are linked by name, birth year, Irish birth, and above all by the Bible's provenance through Patrick's own daughter; the censuses show a boy of the right age with Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County in 1850 and 1860.

## Conflict
Conflict c_001 concerns birthplace: the censuses say Ireland, the death certificate says Pennsylvania. It is resolved in favor of Ireland: the censuses are contemporary, and the 1845 baptism and Bible entry (Ireland) agree, while the death certificate informant was a son-in-law reporting 63 years after the event. The error does not touch the parentage evidence, and every source that names a father names Thomas Flynn. No source contradicts it.

## Scope and limits
Searched: both censuses, death certificate, Schuylkill probate for Thomas Flynn (no records, a negative that does not contradict), the Irish parish register, and the family Bible. Nothing reachable remains that would alter the answer. As with any proof, new evidence could cause reassessment, but none is known.

Tree fact consulted: F1 (Birth, Ireland, about 1845, on I1) agrees with the baptism; F3 (Thomas Flynn, Birth, about 1818, Ireland) is a starting-tree fact with no linked source entry in research.json.

Tier: proved. Two independent original sources with primary information agree, the one conflict is resolved, and the search was reasonably exhaustive.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.
